problem/task: Say you want a network that tells ten kinds of flower apart, and you have a few hundred photos. Each comes with its label: the right answer, the flower's name, written down by a person.
problem/many: But a ConvNet has millions of weights. Trained from scratch on so few photos, it memorizes them: the training loss falls while the validation loss climbs. It overfits.
problem/imagenet: Far bigger sets exist. In 2009, Jia Deng, Fei-Fei Li and colleagues introduced ImageNet, a vast collection of labeled photos. Its yearly contest used about one point two million of them, in a thousand classes.
problem/pretrained: Networks trained on it are free to download. They are pretrained: trained before, on another task. Can one of them help with your flowers?
layers/l1: Look inside one, from the image up. The first layer's filters respond to edges at many angles, and to blobs of color.
layers/mid: In 2013, Matthew Zeiler and Rob Fergus pictured what the layers above respond to: combinations of those, then textures, then parts, such as eyes and legs.
layers/last: The last layer is a linear classifier. It reads five hundred and twelve features: numbers that describe the image, as before, only now computed by the layers below. It scores ImageNet's thousand classes.
layers/yosinski: In 2014, Jason Yosinski and colleagues measured how well each layer carries over to a new task. The first layers are general, since edges and colors are in nearly every photo. Higher layers grow specific to their old classes.
layers/asis: So the network cannot be used as it is: its last layer scores ImageNet's classes, not your ten.
swap/freeze: Instead, keep its layers, and freeze them. Setting requires grad to false means no gradient is computed for a weight, so gradient descent never moves it.
swap/swap: Then swap the last layer for a new one: five hundred and twelve features in, ten scores out, one per flower.
swap/count: It has five hundred and twelve times ten weights, plus ten biases: five thousand one hundred and thirty parameters. Only those are handed to gradient descent.
swap/fit: Thousands of numbers, not millions: a few hundred photos can fit them without memorizing.
swap/two: With two new layers, count each one the same way: its weights, plus one bias per output.
swap/razavian: In 2014, Ali Sharif Razavian and colleagues did just this, with an ImageNet network and a linear classifier on top. On scenes, birds and flowers, it rivaled or beat methods built for each task.
swap/name: This is transfer learning: what one task learned is carried over, or transferred, to another.
howmuch/more: A few hundred photos: train only the new layer. Tens of thousands: unfreeze every layer, and keep training, starting from the pretrained weights instead of random ones.
howmuch/tune: That is fine-tuning. The weights are nearly right already, and training only adjusts them a little, like tuning a guitar string that is almost in pitch.
howmuch/lr: So fine-tune with a small learning rate, often a tenth of the one used from scratch: here, zero point zero one becomes zero point zero zero one.
howmuch/why: The pretrained weights already sit near the bottom of the loss. Big steps would overshoot, throwing away what was learned. Small steps keep them close.
howmuch/scratch: With a million photos, you could start from random weights. But Yosinski's team found that transferred weights gave a boost that lasted, even after fine-tuning.
howmuch/xray: And when your images look nothing like photos, say chest X-rays, the early layers carry over best: edges are everywhere. Retrain the top layers, as far down as your data allows.
